title: Copper Mountain Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Copper Mountain wells have a 110-foot median depth; see local yields, water levels, drilling costs, and risks before buying.
h1: Copper Mountain Well Depth, Yield, and Drilling Costs
intro_html:
Buying land or a home near Copper Mountain means understanding the local bedrock, not just finding a permit on a map. DWR records within 5 miles show how deep documented wells were drilled, what reported wells produced, and what a new well may cost in fractured mountain ground.

The records are useful but incomplete: 124 permits are on file, while 48 wells are recorded as constructed. Only 41 report total depth, 17 report pump yield, and 4 report static water level. Treat these figures as a local planning guide, then have a driller evaluate the specific lot.

sections.heading: Copper Mountain well depth is usually moderate, but bedrock controls the bid
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Copper Mountain is 110 feet. The middle half runs from 71 to 202 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 350 feet. That spread matters when comparing drilling proposals: a bid based on 110 feet may not cover a location that encounters less productive fractured granite or gneiss.

Depth records show 41% of wells under 100 feet and 46% between 100 and 300 feet. Another 12% fall between 300 and 600 feet, with no recorded wells at 600 feet or deeper. Most permits identify an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer, so nearby depth is helpful context, not a guarantee for the lot you are buying.

sections.heading: Reported Copper Mountain yields are generally workable, with limited testing
sections.html:
The median reported pump yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half spans 9.4 to 20.0 gallons per minute. Of the wells with yield data, 47% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute and another 47% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Six percent report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, and none report under 1 gallon per minute.

That is a favorable local record, but only 17 wells report a pump yield. A buyer should not treat the median as a promise from a new hole. Ask for the completion report and pumping test, confirm the intended household demand, and make sure the storage tank and pump are sized for the actual result.

sections.heading: Copper Mountain water levels are shallow in the limited records
sections.html:
Only 4 permitted wells near Copper Mountain report a static water level, so there is not enough information here to establish a reliable long-term trend. The median depth to static water is 24 feet, with a middle half from 12 to 74 feet.

Those measurements suggest water can occur relatively close to the surface in some local wells, but they do not prove that every parcel will have the same water level. Static level also differs from a pumping level. Before closing, obtain neighboring well records where available and ask the driller how seasonal recharge, fractured rock, and the proposed well location may affect the result.

sections.heading: Permit history reaches back to the 1960s, with activity in recent years
sections.html:
DWR permit records show 2 permits from the 1960s, 16 from the 1970s, 10 from the 1980s, 41 from the 1990s, 7 from the 2000s, 18 from the 2010s, and 8 from the 2020s. The newest permit year in this data is 2022. The record is therefore not limited to one construction period, but the total number of construction and yield reports is smaller than the permit count.

The most active listed driller is Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 35 records. Buena Vista Drilling (Shelton, William L) has 10, and Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation (Shelton, Joe Wayne) has 4. Confirm current licensing, availability, and scope directly before selecting a contractor.

sections.heading: A median-depth Copper Mountain well may cost $13,200 to $23,000 finished
sections.html:
Local drilling is priced for fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The stated drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 110-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $7,200 to $11,000. That is only the hole.

A finished system with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $13,200 to $23,000 at the median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, casing or grouting requirements, and site-specific electrical or trench work can move the final number. Have bids state the assumed footage and identify what happens if the driller must continue beyond that assumption.

sections.heading: Mine features, septic layout, and low-yield risk need a site review
sections.html:
Within about 10 miles, the mapped environmental record includes 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1416 historic mine features, and 10 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These listings do not automatically mean a particular parcel has contaminated water, but they are reasons to check the property history, test the well water, and ask about nearby mine workings or disturbed ground.

Fractured rock can produce uneven results, including a low-yield or dry hole even where nearby wells perform well. Septic setbacks, slope, access for a rig, casing and grout, and the location of the house all need to work together. Confirm the DWR permit and water-use rules before construction; an exempt household-use well is not permission to use water for every purpose.

sections.heading: What to verify before buying or building near Copper Mountain
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then review every nearby DWR permit and available construction report. Compare recorded depths, yields, aquifer descriptions, and static levels rather than relying on one favorable well. In this area, the fractured-bedrock setting makes the driller’s proposed location and access route important parts of the decision.

For an existing home, request recent water testing, pump information, storage details, and repair history. For vacant land, get a written well estimate based on the access plan and likely depth, plus a septic evaluation before committing to a building layout. If the intended use involves more than ordinary household service, verify the permit limitations and any need for an augmentation plan in an over-appropriated basin.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Copper Mountain?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Copper Mountain is 110 feet. The middle half of reported depths is 71 to 202 feet, while the deepest record reaches 350 feet. Records show 41% under 100 feet and 46% between 100 and 300 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss make the exact depth parcel-specific.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Copper Mountain?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At the 110-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $7,200 to $11,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $13,200 to $23,000. A deeper hole or difficult access can increase the total.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Copper Mountain?
faq.a: Among the 17 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 9.4 to 20.0 gallons per minute. Forty-seven percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 47% report more than 15 gallons per minute. These figures are not a guarantee for a new well.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Copper Mountain?
faq.a: Safety depends on the individual well and its test results. Within about 10 miles, records include 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1416 historic mine features, and 10 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those listings do not prove contamination at a parcel, but buyers should test existing wells and investigate nearby mining and cleanup history.

faq.q: Are Copper Mountain wells in granite or an aquifer?
faq.a: Most permits identify an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 114 wells listed that way. Only 1 well is identified as alluvial, and 0% are Denver Basin aquifer wells. In practical terms, local production commonly depends on fractures in mountain granite or gneiss, so nearby well results help with planning but cannot guarantee the result on another lot.
